Where it began

Blessing Muzarabani was born on 2 October 1996 and grew up in Highfield, a suburb of Harare. He was seven when he first went along to train at Takashinga Cricket Club, and it was there that coaches noticed what he could do.

His big chance came in 2017. Tatenda Taibu picked him for the Rising Stars Academy, and with them he spent three months touring England. Two days after his birthday that October, Rising Stars gave him his first-class debut in the Logan Cup.

The player

Things then moved very quickly indeed. Less than three months after his first-class debut he was a Test cricketer, lining up in a one-off Boxing Day Test with South Africa in 2017. His first one-day international followed against Bangladesh in January 2018, and his first Twenty20 international against Afghanistan the month after. When the 2018 World Cup Qualifier was over, the ICC picked him out as the rising star of Zimbabwe's squad.

He spent the next stage of his career in England with Northamptonshire before coming back to the Zimbabwe side, and later played his domestic cricket for the Southern Rocks. By November 2026 he had played 20 Tests, taking 74 wickets at 26.14 apiece, with three five-wicket hauls and a best of 7 for 58.

What made him special

He made a habit of rising to the big occasion. Against Pakistan in November 2020 he took his first five-wicket haul in one-day internationals, then claimed two more wickets in the super over for good measure. In 2021 he joined Multan Sultans part-way through the Pakistan Super League, took ten wickets in six games and helped them to their first title.

Then came February 2026 and the T20 World Cup. His spell of 4 for 17 against Australia set up a famous 23-run win for Zimbabwe, and along the way he became only the third Zimbabwean, after Richard Ngarava and Sikandar Raza, to reach 100 wickets in T20 internationals.

With the bat

Batting was a more modest business. By November 2026 he had made 293 Test runs at 11.72, with nine not-outs in 34 innings. His top score of 47 left him three short of a fifty, near enough to a half-century to make any lower-order batsman wince in sympathy. He had also held three catches in Tests.

And finally

Most Test careers begin with a long apprenticeship in the domestic game. His began with a single first-class season that had barely got going: he went from a Logan Cup debut to a Boxing Day Test inside three months, which is about as quick as cricket allows.
